text: ServiceNow records field-level change history in a dedicated table, sys_audit. When an audited field changes, an entry captures what it was, what it became, who changed it, and when — the same kind of durable, queryable trail Lesson 18 argued security_admin elevation events deserve.

It's easy to assume that if sys_audit exists, every field change on every table is already being captured. It isn't. Which tables and fields actually get written to sys_audit is a configuration decision, set through each field's Dictionary entry, not a platform default that covers everything automatically.

A field with auditing turned off can change freely, over and over, with no sys_audit entry ever created for it. No amount of querying sys_audit after the fact recovers history that was never captured in the first place.

The obvious instinct is to turn auditing on for every field, on every table, just in case. That runs into a real cost: every additional audited field means every update to it, across every record, writes another sys_audit row. At production scale, that compounds into real storage growth and write overhead.

And it's overhead for change history that, realistically, almost nobody ever queries or reviews. Auditing is not a free safety net just because the mechanism exists — a well-implemented instance audits selectively, not everything by default.

The decision gets made field by field, around one question: would someone genuinely need this field's change history for a compliance requirement, a security investigation, or a dispute over what a record said at a given time? Sensitive personal data, financial amounts, approval states, and role or ACL settings typically clear that bar. Routine metadata usually doesn't.

This is the same discipline Lesson 18 asked for with elevation — track the things that genuinely carry risk, and make sure that tracking is real when it's needed. Lesson 20 picks this up directly: several compliance frameworks explicitly expect a real, selective, defensible audit trail, not a blanket claim that everything is logged somewhere.
